title: GadIR: A Spatial-Topology Preserving Compiler for Quantum Many-Body Systems Simulation
authors: Xiangyu Ren, Yuexun Huang, Zhaohui Yang, Yuchen Zhu, Tsung-Wei Huang, Tsung-Yi Ho, Zhiding Liang, Antonio Barbalace
abstract: Simulating quantum many-body systems has been one of the most important applications of quantum computation. For simulation, the Hamiltonian of a physical system is compiled into quantum programs with native instructions for quantum hardware. In previous works, the Hamiltonian is represented as Pauli strings, then compiled and optimized based on the quantum circuit model. Such representation paradigm neglects the spatial topology of original physical models, which is vital information to reducing the overhead of compiling many-body systems Hamiltonians.   To address such neglect, we introduce a spatial-topology preserving compiler for quantum many-body simulation. Using Pauli gadgets as the representations of the Hamiltonian, we introduce our intermediate representation -- GadIR, to preserve the spatial-topology information of original physical models. Our compiler frontend performs the group reduction algorithm based on Pauli gadget model, which is a hardware-independent optimization. Our compiler backend performs trotterization and scheduling on Pauli gadgets, then synthesizes the Pauli gadgets into hardware-native quantum programs. We evaluate our compiler on all the canonical quantum many-body system models, while achieving a significant reduction on compilation overhead regarding four major quantum architectures. Overall, our spatial-topology preserving IR exploits the compilation optimization space for quantum many-body systems Hamiltonian.
summary: This paper introduces GadIR, a novel intermediate representation designed to compile quantum many-body Hamiltonians while explicitly preserving the underlying spatial topology of the physical system. By using Pauli gadgets, the compiler frontend performs hardware-agnostic group reductions, leading to significant reductions in circuit overhead when synthesizing programs for various quantum hardware architectures.
main_problem: The core problem is efficiently compiling the Hamiltonians of quantum many-body systems into quantum circuits suitable for diverse quantum hardware architectures.
main_result: The proposed compiler, utilizing GadIR, achieves a significant reduction in compilation overhead across multiple quantum hardware platforms compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
method: The authors introduce GadIR, a Pauli gadget-based intermediate representation that explicitly preserves the spatial topology of the physical model. The compiler uses a hardware-independent group reduction frontend and a topology-guided backend for synthesis.
model_or_system: The framework is tested on canonical quantum many-body systems, including the Bose-Hubbard model and Lattice Gauge Theories, which are mapped onto qubit Hamiltonians defined on specific spatial lattices.
key_observables: Compilation overhead reduction (e.g., CNOT/CZ count, depth, non-Clifford gate count) across superconducting, neutral-atom, FTQC, and MBQC backends.
important_parameters: The complexity and structure of the physical Hamiltonian, the specific quantum hardware architecture targeted, and the lattice size/dimensionality.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that preserving the spatial topology via GadIR leads to a more optimized compilation path than standard Pauli string representations. The analysis relies on specific encoding techniques (e.g., Jordan-Wigner) and Trotterization approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow from physical model to Hamiltonian to the GadIR representation, comparing the topological awareness of the proposed method against prior art. Other figures show quantitative comparisons of gate counts and circuit metrics across different hardware backends.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitations of existing Pauli string representations, proposes the GadIR IR to retain spatial topology, details the compiler frontend (group reduction) and backend (Trotterization/scheduling), and validates the approach across multiple physical models and quantum hardware backends.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the crucial bottleneck of mapping complex physical Hamiltonians onto abstract quantum hardware instructions, providing a structured, topology-aware compilation pipeline relevant to all quantum simulation efforts.
